profile.summary: 1 John is a pastoral letter that applies the apostolic witness on Jesus Christ to the concrete life of believers. Its focus is to show that true faith can be recognized in practice: in communion with God, in confession of sin, in brotherly love, in permanence in Christ, and in discernment against false teachings. The letter combats a rupture within the Christian community and reaffirms that knowing God produces life shaped by truth, obedience and love.
profile.setting: The letter was written to churches under the care of John in the Roman province of Asia, probably between the years 85 and 90 AD, after John's ministry in Jerusalem and his move to that region. The background includes increasing persecution of the church, the destruction of Jerusalem and the emergence of a rival group that has departed from apostolic communion. This group spread ideas that would later be associated with Gnosticism, denying, among other things, the full incarnation of Jesus. The authorship is generally attributed to the apostle John, although some scholars propose a presbyterian John; the introduction provided understands that there are strong reasons to see both as the same person.

structure.label: Prologue about the apostolic testimony
structure.description: The letter opens with the statement that the author announces what he has heard, saw and touched about the Word of life, establishing the basis of authority and communion.

structure.label: God is light and life in communion
structure.description: John exposes the relationship between walking in the light, confessing sin and remaining in communion with God and with the brethren.

structure.label: Membership, purity and brotherly love
structure.description: The chapter develops the identity of the children of God, the call to sanctification, and the commandment to love one another in a practical way.

structure.label: Spiritual Discernment and Love that comes from God
structure.description: The letter deals with the test of spirits, the truth about Christ and the inseparable connection between confessing Jesus correctly and loving the brethren.

structure.label: Faith in Jesus, the certainty of eternal life and conclusion
structure.description: John ends by strengthening faith in the Son of God, the security of eternal life and the need to remain faithful to the true God.

themes: The certainty of eternal life in Christ
The True Incarnation and Identity of Jesus as the Son of God
Christian Love as Evidence of Communion with God
Fidelity to apostolic teaching before false teachers
Spiritual Discernment by the Holy Spirit
readingKeys: Notice how John links doctrine and practice: what is believed about Jesus directly affects how one lives.
Note the tests of spiritual authenticity throughout the letter: truth, obedience, love and permanence.
Read carefully the recurring contrasts between light and darkness, truth and lie, children of God and false teachers.
profile.cautions: The exact authorship and date are not consensual in all studies, although the most common view among evangelicals ascribes the letter to the apostle John at the end of the first century. The outstanding introduction combats a kind of teaching that denied true humanity and the full divinity of Christ; in reading the letter, it is appropriate to avoid reducing its warnings only to abstract debates, because John deals with a real crisis of communion and fidelity to the apostolic message.

dossier.narratedEra: End of the apostolic era, with the backdrop of the destruction of Jerusalem and the expansion of the church to the Roman province of Asia. The notes place the community of 1 John between John's late ministry and the crisis of false teachers within the churches linked to him.
dossier.compositionEra: Probably between about A.D. 85-90, after the gospel of John and after the migration from John to the Roman province of Asia. The sources also present an alternative academic proposal authored by a "presbyter John," but point out that many evangelicals identify him with the apostle John.

politics.title: Increasing persecution and exit of Jerusalem
politics.detail: Tyndale's notes situate John and the other apostles as probably forced to leave Jerusalem around 68, or rather, due to increased persecution of the church and the siege of Jerusalem by the Roman armies.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read 1 John as a letter of pastoral consolidation after displacement and external pressure: the exhortation to permanence in apostolic communion is not born in abstract, but in context of crisis and dispersion.

politics.title: Roman Province of Asia as a new ministry camp
politics.detail: After Jerusalem, John would have migrated to the Roman province of Asia (Western region of present-day Turkey) and exercised a successful ministry there, especially among Gentiles.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of 1 John gains a missionary and community horizon: the letter deals not only with an isolated local church, but of networks of communities under apostolic influence in Roman Asia.
politics.reference: Introduction; implicit recipients and "churches under John's care."

politics.title: Churches under the care of John and probable regional circulation
politics.detail: Matthew Henry describes the epistle as a circular letter sent to various churches, and Tyndale states that she was sent to the churches under the care of John, including those mentioned in Revelation 1:11.
politics.readingImpact: The reader must understand the warnings and exhortations as valid for a network of churches, not just for a single group; this reinforces the character of public instruction and defense of the common faith.
politics.reference: Introduction; relation to Revelation 1:11 and circular character of the letter.

politics.title: Intra-Community conflict instead of direct imperial dispute
politics.detail: The sources do not describe a detailed imperial policy, but show an internal rupture: some members left the Christian community to form a rival group with teaching considered heretical.
politics.readingImpact: The focus of the letter is not resistance to the State, but discernment and fidelity within the community; the most visible "political" in 1 John is ecclesial, linked to the communion and separation of false teachers.

customs.title: Community life marked by communion and permanence in apostolic teaching
customs.detail: The notes repeat that communion with God passes through communion with the apostles and with the brethren. Entering and remaining in this communion is presented as a concrete practice of Christian life.
customs.readingImpact: The letter should be read as a manual of community life: true faith appears in bond, perseverance and submission to the received teaching, not in individualistic spirituality.

customs.title: Confession of sins as an ordinary spiritual practice
customs.detail: In 1:8-10, confession to God is described as necessary to maintain continuous communion with him. The notes assume that Christians still sin and need to confess, without denying the reality of the new life.
customs.readingImpact: This prevents a moralistic or triumphalistic reading: the reading of 1 John must include regular repentance, dependence on the righteousness of Christ and an honest examination of one's own life.

customs.title: Concrete love expressed in sacrifice and material care
customs.detail: Tyndale defines Christian love in 3:16-18 as sacrificial action: giving time, effort, prayer, goods and even life to supply other people's needs.
customs.readingImpact: The exhortation to love in 1 John is not abstract feeling; the context makes reading practical, ethical and community, requiring concrete gestures in favor of the brethren.

customs.title: Fellowship as a visible belonging to the people of God
customs.detail: The note of 1:3 explains that "vossus/ our communion" includes entering into the communion of the apostles by association with them as they live, or today by staying in their teaching; whoever breaks this communion shows himself outside of the family of God.
customs.readingImpact: The reading of the letter gains a social and ecclesial criterion: "communion" is not mere inner experience, but visible and faithful belonging to the apostolic community.

language.title: Poetic prologue in parallel to the Gospel of John
language.detail: 1:1-4 is described as a poetic prologue that reflects the prologue of the Gospel of John. The notes insist on literary and theological continuity between gospel and epistle.
language.readingImpact: The reader must treat the opening of 1 John as a solemn introduction, not only as a greeting; the style reinforces witness, revelation and communion.

language.title: We are apostolic and language of eyewitness
language.detail: The "we" in 1:1-4 is explained as a reference to John and the other apostles, and possibly to other Christians who saw and touched Jesus. Matthew Henry highlights the weight of the "hearing," we saw, contemplate and our hands touch.
language.readingImpact: Language is not only devotional; it establishes witness authority. The letter must be read as a defense of the real incarnation against teachings that denied the true humanity of Christ.

language.title: "Light" as a moral and revealing metaphor
language.detail: In 1:5-7, "Light" represents the holiness and revelation of God; it is the opposite of falsehood and disorderly life, called "trevas."
language.readingImpact: This guides the ethical reading of the letter: walking in the light means living in a way consistent with the character of God, and not just adhere to correct formulas.

language.title: "Remain" as a faithful continuity, not mere static state
language.detail: In 3:6, the Greek verb men is explained as "abiding"/remaining," in contrast to moving away to falsehood. Persisting in sin contradicts this permanence.
language.readingImpact: The term helps to read the letter as called relational and doctrinal continuity; to remain in Christ includes practical fidelity and perseverance in apostolic teaching.

language.title: Water and blood as an antiheretic Christological formula
language.detail: In 5:6-8, water and blood are attached to the baptism and cross of Christ. The note identifies a direct refutation of heresy associated with Cerinthus: the Christ would have descended into baptism and left before death.
language.readingImpact: This language should be read as a statement of the continuous identity of Jesus as Christ and the Son of God, from beginning to the end of his work, without separating the human Jesus from a spiritual Christ.

language.title: "Anticrist", "false prophets" and "dolos" as categories of discernment
language.detail: The notes use "antichrist" for those who deny the true humanity and/or full divinity of Jesus, and in 5:21 "idolos" is understood, in the context of the letter, as any false teaching that deviates from Christ.
language.readingImpact: These terms show that the letter has a vocabulary of spiritual discernment: not every religious speech is reliable, and the reader should evaluate doctrines by apostolic witness.

timeline.title: Roman Siege of Jerusalem and Probable Apostolic Displacement
timeline.detail: The notes place the departure of John and the other apostles from Jerusalem around AD 68, or rather because of increasing persecution and the Roman siege.
timeline.readingImpact: The letter arises after historical trauma and ministerial displacement, which explains the emphasis on remaining in the truth received and not to be carried away by new masters.

timeline.title: Migration from John to Roman Asia after the fall of Jerusalem
timeline.detail: Tyndale claims that John would have migrated to the Roman province of Asia some time later, probably after A.D. 70.
timeline.readingImpact: This anchors 1 John at a late stage of the Jordanian ministry, when the apostolic instruction already needed to be preserved against internal distortions.

timeline.title: Writing of the Gospel of John before 1 John
timeline.detail: Tyndale's introduction says that by A.D. 90, John had already written his Gospel to these believers.
timeline.readingImpact: The close relationship between the Gospel and the epistle helps the reader to see 1 John as a natural extension of the Joanine theology, especially about incarnation, life and communion.

timeline.title: Letter to the churches of Asia about AD 85-90
timeline.detail: The notes state that the first letter was sent to the churches under the care of John, in the range of AD 85-90.
timeline.readingImpact: The approximate date reinforces that the document responds to a mature crisis: false doctrines had already penetrated and demanded reaffirmation of the apostolic nucleus.

timeline.title: Break with rival group and echo of heresies of gnostic type
timeline.detail: After the writing of the Gospel, some Christians withdrew to form a rival group. The notes describe this group as heretical, with characteristics that would later be called Gnosticism, including denying that Jesus came in the flesh.
timeline.readingImpact: The letter is best read in response to a split already under way; his warnings about lies, darkness, antichrists, and denial of Christ gain concrete historical weight.

investigation: The traditional apostolic authorship is supported by Tyndale and Matthew Henry, but Tyndale recognizes the academic proposal of a "John the priest"; the notes argue that both are probably the same man.
The letter is treated as circular and addressed to churches in Asia, but the sources do not accurately identify all receiving communities beyond the general mention of the churches under John's care.

The connection with Cerinto and an initial form of docetism/gnosticism is presented as possible and useful for reading, but the formulation remains identified as "may have"/"be," so it is not absolute historical certainty.
The sources offer little political information beyond the siege of Jerusalem, persecution and the Roman province of Asia; there are no names of emperors or specific political disputes.
There is mention of Papias' tradition via Eusebius, but the interpretation of this testimony is discussed; the dossier does not resolve the controversy, only records it according to the notes.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the attached notes and therefore reflects a selective and confessionally evangelical coverage of the text. There were no gaps with external research or detailed chronologies outside what the sources explain. The political section is limited because the notes almost do not deal with appointed rulers, institutions or imperial events beyond the siege of Jerusalem, persecution and the Roman province of Asia. The sections of customs and language are also restricted to what the notes really comment on: communion, confession, sacrificial love, permanence, light/thirties, eyewitness, water and blood, antichrist and idols. Textual questions such as the long interpolation of 1 John 5:7 are mentioned only as a late variant, without extrapolating beyond the material provided. When there are alternative proposals of authorship or context, they were marked as debated or interpretative, without treating them as independent historical proof.
